Who breathes shipping emissions near Long Beach?

San Pedro Bay pilot: how far can emissions and wind be aggregated before exposure estimates degrade?

Author
Affiliation

Jeremy Proville

Environmental Defense Fund

Published

Last updated 2026-11-24

NoteWork in progress

This is a first pass at the 0.25° resolution of the gridded emissions, with a simple screening model of dispersion. Read the results as comparisons between ways of aggregating the data, not as estimates of absolute concentrations. Numbers will move as the emissions grid and other inputs are refined.

This notebook builds on the gridded shipping emissions near Long Beach and asks who breathes them. The pilot’s question is how far emissions and wind can be aggregated, in time and in space, before estimates of population exposure degrade. The answer sets the resolution a wider analysis can rest on: joining hourly emissions to hourly wind is affordable for one box, but not for every port in the world.

We use emLab’s hourly PM2.5 emissions for the 20 ERA5 grid cells of the study area in 2025 (372.9 metric tonnes in total), ERA5’s hourly wind and boundary layer height at the same grid points, and a population grid of 0.01° (about 1 km) pixels covering the box and about 50 km beyond it on every side, where 20.6 million people live. A simple plume model turns emissions and wind into an annual mean concentration at every populated pixel. We run it once with everything hourly (the reference) and then with emissions and wind aggregated in different ways, and we measure how far each result moves from the reference.

Findings so far

  1. When ships emit barely matters. Daily, monthly or annual emissions give the same population exposure as hourly emissions, within 2%. Emissions near the ports are steady through the day, so annual or monthly totals are enough.
  2. How the wind is summarized matters a lot. A wind rose that keeps the dilution of each wind direction stays within 2% of the reference. Averaging wind speed and mixing height on their own changes exposure by −60%. Ignoring wind direction gets the regional average roughly right (−13%) but misses 32% of the most exposed people.
  3. Where emissions sit inside a 0.25° cell matters most near the port. Across the region, the spatial choices move exposure by 15% to 25%. Within 10 km of the port, they multiply it by 1.5× to 2.8×. A single regional average hides this, so results should be scored near the port and for the most exposed people, not with one number.
  4. A single port point gets time right but collapses space. Putting all emissions at the Port of Long Beach with monthly wind roses changes regional exposure by +25%, and multiplies exposure within 5 km by 2.8×.
  5. A distance buffer misses most of the people the plume reaches. Of the 109,869 people the model ranks most exposed (as many as live within 5 km of the ports), only 13% live within 5 km. With all emissions at a single port point the share is still 19%, so the gap comes from the wind, not only from where the emissions sit.
  6. Passenger vessels nearly at rest drive about half of exposure. Passenger-class vessels moving at under 1 knot make 47% of the box’s PM2.5 and 48% of population exposure, mostly in cells with marinas. They look like many small moored boats, each emitting little, rather than cruise ships, so how the emissions model treats small craft at berth is one of the largest sensitivities in this notebook.

The exposure model

The model is deliberately simple: the point is to compare aggregation choices on equal terms. Each hour, a source’s emissions Q blow towards the 22.5° sector the wind points to and mix evenly through the boundary layer, so the concentration at distance r in that sector is C = Q / (Δθ · r · u · H), where u is the wind speed, H the boundary layer height and Δθ = 2π / 16. The annual mean concentration at each pixel sums this over every hour and every source. It covers primary PM2.5 only, with no chemistry, deposition or terrain.

  • Reference. Hourly emissions in each of the 20 cells, with that hour’s ERA5 10 m wind at the cell’s grid point (valid at the start of the hour, as the data README recommends). Ships are on water, but where on the water is unknown at 0.25°, so each cell’s emissions are spread evenly over the water in the cell (ESA WorldCover).
  • Details. The plume’s angular profile is triangular, so it blends smoothly between neighboring sectors (a hard-edged sector draws spokes from point sources). Wind speed, boundary layer height and distance have floors of 0.5 m/s, 50 m and 1 km. There is no distance cutoff.
  • Receptors. Every 0.01° pixel with people (WorldPop Global2, 2025).
  • Metrics. Each variant is compared with the reference on three measures:
    • Change in exposure: the population-weighted mean concentration, relative to the reference.
    • Neighborhood error: the people-weighted mean absolute difference at the pixel level, as a share of the reference. It catches errors that cancel out in the regional mean.
    • Most exposed 10% kept: the share of the 10% of people most exposed in the reference who are still in the top 10% under the variant.
NoteShow code: the plume model

u, v and blh are hourly ERA5 10 m wind components (m/s) and boundary layer height (m) at each cell’s grid point, as arrays of cell × hour. geometry() gives, for one source, the weight of each of the 16 wind sectors at each receptor pixel (km_offsets() turns degrees into km east and north); concentration() combines it with the wind rose weights W[s, k] shown under the aggregation ladder.

pilot/footprint.py
N_SECTORS = 16
DTHETA = 2 * np.pi / N_SECTORS
MIN_SPEED_M_S = 0.5
MIN_BLH_M = 50.0
R_MIN_KM = 1.0
R_MAX_KM = np.inf  # no per-source cutoff: a 50 km cutoff drew arcs that differed between geometries (2026-11-24)
UG_PER_KG = 1e9
S_PER_H = 3600.0


def sector_and_dilution(u, v, blh):
    """Sector the wind blows towards (0 = north, clockwise) and 1 / (u H) in s/m2, with floors."""
    towards_deg = np.degrees(np.arctan2(u, v)) % 360.0
    k = (((towards_deg + 180.0 / N_SECTORS) % 360.0) // (360.0 / N_SECTORS)).astype(int)
    speed = np.maximum(np.hypot(u, v), MIN_SPEED_M_S)
    height = np.maximum(blh, MIN_BLH_M)
    return k, 1.0 / (speed * height), speed, height


def geometry(src_lon, src_lat, src_w, rec_lon, rec_lat, chunk=64):
    """B[k, r] for one source made of weighted sub-sources: sum_j w_j * 1[sector] / (dtheta * r_m)."""
    n_rec = len(rec_lon)
    b = np.zeros(N_SECTORS * n_rec)
    near = np.zeros(n_rec)
    rec_ix = np.arange(n_rec)
    for a in range(0, len(src_lon), chunk):
        sl, sb, sw = src_lon[a:a + chunk], src_lat[a:a + chunk], src_w[a:a + chunk]
        dx, dy = km_offsets(sl, sb, rec_lon, rec_lat)
        r = np.hypot(dx, dy)
        # Triangular angular profile: a receptor between two sector centres takes both sectors' weights, linearly.
        # Same integral as the 22.5 degree top-hat, but point sources don't draw spokes at sector edges.
        pos = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(dx, dy)) % 360.0) / (360.0 / N_SECTORS)
        k0 = np.floor(pos).astype(int) % N_SECTORS
        frac = pos - np.floor(pos)
        val = sw[:, None] / (DTHETA * np.maximum(r, R_MIN_KM) * 1000.0)
        val[r > R_MAX_KM] = 0.0
        is_near = r < R_MIN_KM
        # Within the distance floor the source surrounds the receptor: count it in every sector equally
        near += np.bincount(np.broadcast_to(rec_ix, r.shape)[is_near], weights=val[is_near], minlength=n_rec)
        val[is_near] = 0.0
        for kk, wt in [(k0, 1.0 - frac), ((k0 + 1) % N_SECTORS, frac)]:
            b += np.bincount((kk * n_rec + rec_ix[None, :]).ravel(), weights=(val * wt).ravel(),
                             minlength=N_SECTORS * n_rec)
    return b.reshape(N_SECTORS, n_rec) + near[None, :] / N_SECTORS


def concentration(w, b):
    """ug/m3 at each receptor from W[s, k] (kg/h * s/m2) and B[s, k, r] (1/m)."""
    return np.einsum("sk,skr->r", w, b) * UG_PER_KG / S_PER_H

In the reference, the population-weighted mean concentration is 0.20 µg/m³ across the region, rising to 0.61-0.67 µg/m³ within 10 km of the port (Figure 1).

Aggregation ladder

Each variant changes one thing and keeps everything else as in the reference (Figure 2, Table 1). The time variants replace hourly emissions with daily, monthly or annual means. The wind variants try different ways of summarizing a year of hourly wind. The space variants move where the emissions sit. The sensitivities change an input.

The wind rose used in the time variants is weighted by dilution: for each of 16 directions, it keeps the sum of 1/(u · H) over the hours the wind blows that way, not just the number of hours. Because the model depends on each hour only through its direction and 1/(u · H), annual emissions with this rose would reproduce the hourly result exactly if emissions were constant, and come close whenever emissions don’t move with the wind.

NoteShow code: dilution-weighted wind roses and the time and wind variants

q[s, h] is PM2.5 (kg) emitted in cell s in hour h, k[s, h] the sector the wind blows towards and d[s, h] = 1/(u · H). Each variant returns W[s, k]: emissions times dilution, summed by sector and averaged over the year.

pilot/footprint.py
def weights(q, k, d):
    n = q.shape[1]
    return np.stack([np.bincount(k[s], weights=q[s] * d[s], minlength=N_SECTORS) / n for s in range(q.shape[0])])


def block_mean(q, labels):
    """Replace each hour's emissions by the mean over its block (day or month)."""
    out = np.empty_like(q)
    for lab in np.unique(labels):
        sel = labels == lab
        out[:, sel] = q[:, sel].mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return out


def temporal_variants(q, k, d, speed, height, day, month):
    n = q.shape[1]
    q_bar = q.mean(axis=1)
    freq = np.stack([np.bincount(k[s], minlength=N_SECTORS) / n for s in range(q.shape[0])])
    return {
        "hourly": weights(q, k, d),
        "daily": weights(block_mean(q, day), k, d),
        "monthly": weights(block_mean(q, month), k, d),
        "annual": weights(np.repeat(q_bar[:, None], n, axis=1), k, d),
        "annual_freq_rose": q_bar[:, None] * freq * d.mean(axis=1)[:, None],
        "annual_freq_rose_mean_wind": q_bar[:, None] * freq / (speed.mean(axis=1) * height.mean(axis=1))[:, None],
        "annual_no_direction": np.repeat((q_bar * d.mean(axis=1))[:, None] / N_SECTORS, N_SECTORS, axis=1),
    }

When ships emit

Emissions in the port cell vary only between 0.86 and 1.14 times their annual mean across the hours of the day (Figure 3, right). With emissions this steady, and with a wind rose that keeps each direction’s dilution, aggregating emissions in time costs almost nothing: +2% for daily means, +2% for monthly and +2% for annual. Monthly or annual emissions, which a global analysis can afford, are enough.

How the wind is summarized

At the port cell, the plume heads inland (towards the west-northwest through east-northeast) in 71% of hours, peaking at 89% around 13:00 Pacific Standard Time with the afternoon sea breeze. Those are also the hours when the wind is strong and the boundary layer deep: 1/(u · H) falls to 0.2 of its annual mean in the early afternoon and sits at 1.5-1.8 times the mean at night, when the plume more often heads out to sea. Over the year, hours with the plume heading inland have 0.78 of the mean dilution term, and hours heading out to sea 1.53.

This coupling between direction and dilution is what the wind summary has to keep:

  • The dilution-weighted wind rose keeps it, and lands within 2%.
  • Averaging direction and dilution separately (the share of hours in each direction times the annual mean of 1/(u · H)) sends poorly diluted night-time air inland: +37%.
  • Multiplying the share of hours by the mean wind speed and mean mixing height: −60%. Calm hours with a shallow boundary layer dominate 1/(u · H), and averaging u and H first discards them.
  • Ignoring direction altogether: −13% across the region, but a neighborhood error of 20%, and 32% of the most exposed people are misidentified.
  • Wind at 100 m instead of 10 m: −9% (stronger winds). A second-order choice; we keep 10 m.

Where emissions sit inside a cell

At 0.25° we know how much each cell emits but not where in the cell. Two placements are equally defensible: spread over the cell’s water (the reference) or at the cell’s center point. Across the region they differ by 15%, but within 5 km of the port by 2.2× (Figure 4, Figure 5, Table 2). Cell centers can also land on people: the center of the Seal Beach and Huntington Harbour cell (-118.00, 33.75) is on land, which makes a hotspot no ship causes (Figure 4, bottom left).

NoteShow code: spreading each cell’s emissions over its water

water is the water share (0-1, ESA WorldCover) of each 0.01° pixel. Each 0.25° cell holds 25 × 25 of them; the cell’s emissions are split among its water pixels in proportion to their water.

pilot/footprint.py
HALF_CELL = 0.125


def cell_water_subsources(s, pix_lon, pix_lat, water):
    sel = (np.abs(pix_lon - CELL_LON[s]) < HALF_CELL) & (np.abs(pix_lat - CELL_LAT[s]) < HALF_CELL)
    w = water[sel]
    if sel.sum() != 625:
        sys.exit(f"cell {s}: {sel.sum()} sub-pixels, expected 625")
    w = w / w.sum() if w.sum() > 0 else np.full(w.shape, 1.0 / w.size)
    keep = w > 0
    return pix_lon[sel][keep], pix_lat[sel][keep], w[keep]

Only a finer emissions grid can say which placement is closer to the truth.

A single port point

With emissions only by port, the natural shortcut is to place each port’s emissions at one point and use monthly wind roses. In the study area, this gets time right but collapses space: +25% across the region, 2.8× within 5 km and 2.1× at 5-10 km. Combined with a wind rose times the mean wind speed and mixing height, the error flips sign: −50%. The gridded emissions, or points at anchorages, should do better; a finer grid would show by how much.

Which cells drive exposure

The cell holding both ports has 47% of the box’s emissions and 53% of population exposure (Figure 6). Two cells with small-craft harbors weigh more in exposure than in emissions: Seal Beach and Huntington Harbour (11% of emissions, 18% of exposure; the cell is 81% land, so its water is next to people) and Santa Monica and Marina del Rey (11% and 13%). The cell off Huntington Beach and Newport Beach is 98% water, so spreading its emissions over the water puts Newport Harbor’s emissions offshore: 12% of emissions but 7% of exposure, probably too low.

Much of this comes from passenger-class vessels nearly at rest. Passenger rows averaging under 1 knot hold 176.1 t of PM2.5, 47% of the box total, mostly in these four cells: 51.4 t in the port cell, 37.6 t off Newport, 32.6 t at Santa Monica and 25.4 t at Seal Beach. Together they account for 48% of population exposure (the model is linear in emissions, so this is the change in exposure when they are left out). Many vessels at once, each emitting little, looks more like small moored craft than cruise ships, so these results lean heavily on how the emissions model treats small craft at berth.

Distance buffers versus the plume

Studies of who lives near ports usually draw a buffer around them and count everyone inside as exposed. A buffer ignores the wind. To see what that misses, we compare each buffer with a plume zone of the same size: as many people as live in the buffer, chosen as those with the highest modeled ship PM2.5. If a buffer captured who is exposed, the two would hold the same people.

NoteShow code: the plume zone

c is each pixel’s modeled annual mean ship PM2.5, pop its people and n the number of people in the distance buffer being matched.

pilot/equity.py
def plume_zone(c, pop, n):
    """1 for the n people with the highest modelled ship PM2.5 (fractional at the edge), else 0."""
    order = np.argsort(-c)
    before = np.cumsum(pop[order]) - pop[order]
    x = np.zeros_like(pop)
    x[order] = np.clip((n - before) / np.where(pop[order] > 0, pop[order], 1), 0, 1)
    return x

They hold different people (Figure 7, Table 3). 109,869 people live within 5 km of either port. Of the same number of people most exposed in the model, only 13% live within 5 km. The other 87% live farther out, at a median distance of 6.7 km, east of the ports in Long Beach and towards Seal Beach: 69% of them in the cell holding the ports and 31% in the Seal Beach and Huntington Harbour cell. The buffer instead takes in San Pedro and Wilmington, on the west side of the port complex. At the port cell, the plume heads west through north, towards them, in 22% of hours, and north-northeast through east, towards Long Beach, in 63% (Figure 3). People in the plume zone breathe 0.74 µg/m³ of ship PM2.5 on average, against 0.62 µg/m³ for people within 5 km. The overlap is 0% at 2 km, 63% at 10 km and 74% at 25 km: a buffer only agrees with the plume once it is large enough to take in most of the people the plume reaches.

The wind is the main reason, not just where the emissions sit. If all of the box’s emissions are put at the Port of Long Beach point, so that a circle around the port is the natural buffer, only 19% of the 5 km plume zone still lives within 5 km. Keeping the emissions spread over the water but letting them blow equally in every direction raises the overlap to 54%. Across every variant with wind, the overlap at the 5 km size stays at or below 27%.

Exactly which people fall in a small plume zone is less settled (Table 4). Placing each cell’s emissions at its center point instead of over its water keeps only 6% of the reference 5 km plume zone (62% at 10 km). Dropping passenger vessels at rest matters less (88% kept at 5 km). So the finding that buffers miss most of the most exposed people holds across these choices, but drawing the plume zone person by person needs the finer emissions grid. The comparison also assumes the screening model ranks people correctly, which a full dispersion model would need to confirm.

Who is exposed (in progress)

We are now asking whether vulnerable populations are over-represented among exposed people: young children (under 5), older adults (65 and over) and, once we have a measure that works near the ports, socioeconomically vulnerable populations (see below). For each group, we divide its share among exposed people by its share of the county’s population, so each exposed person is compared with their own county. A ratio of 1 means no disparity. We compare three definitions of who is exposed: living within 1 to 25 km of either port, the plume zone of the same size (previous section), and everyone, weighted by their modeled ship PM2.5.

NoteShow code: the group disproportion ratio

g is the group’s people in each pixel, x each pixel’s exposure weight (1 or 0 for a buffer or plume zone; modeled PM2.5 for the concentration-weighted version), and g_tot, p_tot the group’s and everyone’s totals in each county.

pilot/equity.py
def disproportion(g, x, pop, county, g_tot, p_tot):
    """Group share among exposed vs its county share, pooled with each person's own county as baseline."""
    observed = (g * x).sum()
    expected = 0.0
    for c in np.unique(county):
        sel = county == c
        expected += (pop[sel] * x[sel]).sum() * g_tot[c] / p_tot[c]
    return observed / expected if expected > 0 else np.nan
  • Weighting everyone by concentration gives ratios of about 1 (1.00× for children under 5, 1.00× for adults 65 and over). Ship PM2.5 reaches the whole basin, so the millions of people with low exposure swamp the few with high exposure. It is not a useful disparity measure here.
  • Buffers and plume zones give different answers, because they hold different people. At the 5 km size, adults 65 and over are 1.03× as represented in the buffer as in their county, but 1.40× in the plume zone. For children under 5 the figures are 1.02× and 0.73×. The plume zone leans towards coastal Long Beach and Seal Beach, so this depends on where the emissions near the marinas sit.
WarningPreliminary

First results, not yet checked.

Socioeconomic vulnerability: work in progress

We also want to know whether socioeconomically vulnerable populations are over-represented among exposed people. That needs a measure that ranks neighborhoods correctly within a county. We have tried two global, gridded datasets, and neither passes a simple check in Los Angeles, so neither is used in the results above.

  • GRDI v1 (CIESIN, 2022): a 0-100 index at about 1 km, built from six components: child dependency ratio, infant mortality, subnational Human Development Index, built-up area, night lights, and the trend in night lights.
  • HDI of Sherman et al. (2026): the Human Development Index predicted with machine learning from daytime satellite imagery and night lights (MOSAIKS), released at 0.1° (about 10 km) and scaled so each state matches its Global Data Lab value.

The check ranks people within their county by each layer, from most to least vulnerable, as the analysis would, and looks at where well-known places land (Table 6). Of the 5 affluent places, GRDI puts 3 in their county’s two most deprived fifths and the HDI puts 4 in its two lowest fifths. Of the 5 lower-income places, the HDI puts 3 in its two highest fifths (GRDI puts 1 in its two least deprived), including Wilmington, next to the ports, in the HDI’s highest fifth. Palos Verdes Estates scores 0.935 on the HDI against 0.980 for Wilmington.

Why they fail here:

  • GRDI separates places mainly by built-up area and night lights within a metro area, because its income and health inputs come at state or regional level. Dark, low-density hillside and coastal suburbs then look deprived. Its documentation warns that it “may not fully capture intra-urban differentials in deprivation”. It also shows little difference across the US-Mexico border at the two city pairs we looked at (Table 7).
  • The HDI separates countries well: Tijuana 0.806 against San Diego 0.964, Mexicali 0.851 against El Centro 0.954. Within Los Angeles County, though, 90% of people live where it is between 0.935 and 0.975, a band narrow enough for the model’s errors to set the ranking (its documentation warns of noise and compressed variance). The 0.1° cell holding the ports, Wilmington and San Pedro has the highest value in its area, probably because port infrastructure looks like development in satellite imagery. A 0.1° cell is also larger than the 5 km buffers.
  • Both lean on satellite imagery, which sees density, buildings and light rather than income. GRDI makes dark, leafy suburbs look deprived; the HDI makes the port-industrial area look developed. Either bias distorts a comparison centered on ports, so any global layer needs this kind of check near ports before we use it.

We also looked at a third global layer, Meta’s Relative Wealth Index (Chi et al., 2022), which predicts survey-measured household wealth on 2.4 km tiles from satellite imagery, night lights, mobile networks and Facebook connectivity data. It covers only low- and middle-income countries, so it has no values in the pilot’s US counties and cannot be checked against the places above. In the copy we checked (Earth Engine), ports with at least one of its tiles within 10 km handled 19% of 2024 port-visit ship PM2.5 (11% of the 12,643 ports with emissions). China, missing from that copy, alone handled 30%. Even a release covering every low- and middle-income country could reach at most 58%, since the rest is in high-income countries. That is too little overlap with the world’s ports for a main measure, so we have set it aside.

Next, for the pilot, we will test a US census-tract measure (American Community Survey income or poverty, the CDC Social Vulnerability Index or CalEnviroScreen 4.0) against the same places.

Next steps

  • Keep annual or monthly emissions with dilution-weighted wind roses for the wider analysis.
  • Rerun the spatial variants against a finer emissions grid, if one can be built.
  • Score each variant near the port, for the most exposed people and by group, rather than with one regional average.
  • Define exposure from the plume rather than from distance buffers, and choose how to size the plume zone: matched to buffers, as here, or by a concentration cutoff once a finer grid firms up the pattern near the ports.
  • Find a measure of socioeconomic vulnerability that passes the check near the ports: a census-tract measure for the pilot, and for a wider analysis, the same check of any global layer near ports.

Input Source Used for

Counties US Census TIGER 2018 counties in Earth Engine (TIGER/2018/Counties) County baselines for the group ratios
Socioeconomic vulnerability (tested, not used) GRDI v1 (CIESIN 2022, doi:10.7927/3xxe-ap97), about 1 km; HDI of Sherman et al. 2026, Nature Communications (mosaiks.org/hdi), raster V2.0, 0.1°; both averaged to 0.01° Vulnerability fifths within each county; both failed the sanity check within Los Angeles
Relative wealth (coverage only) Meta’s Relative Wealth Index (Chi et al. 2022, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.2113658119), Earth Engine community catalog copy (projects/sat-io/open-datasets/facebook/relative_wealth_index, updated 2021-04-18); ports and their 2024 port-visit emissions from emLab’s data/gfw/ at commit ac9cddd; World Bank income groups (API) Share of ports and port PM2.5 with RWI tiles within 10 km; not used in the results

Wind is joined to emissions at the same grid point and UTC hour, using the wind valid at the start of the hour in which the emissions occurred, as the data README describes.

Caveats

  • The dispersion model is a screening model: primary PM2.5 only, with no secondary formation, chemistry, deposition or terrain. Absolute concentrations are indicative only. Adding secondary PM2.5, formed from ship NOx and SOx in the atmosphere, is on the to-do list, using InMAP or a similar approach.
  • ERA5’s 0.25° wind smooths the coastal sea breeze, and each cell uses one wind.
  • The population grid stops about 50 km beyond the box, so people farther away are left out, equally for every variant.
  • The emissions inherit the model’s caveats: no shore power at berth, and emissions from AIS gaps lumped into the hour of the first message after the gap.
  • One year (2025) and one pollutant (PM2.5) so far.
  • WorldPop R2025A is an alpha release that may change during its first year.
  • Place names for cells are inferred from their coordinates.
